title: Manas ki jat: one human race
hookLine: recognize all humankind as one (Akal Ustat 85)
carry: recognize one human family under every label

lines: BOX ONE, BOX TWO, BOX THREE.
cards: Forms ask. Box one, box two, box three. Religion, caste, nationality, community.

Hospital intake sheets, school applications, a matchmaker's questions over chai. Sometimes the boxes are there to help. Sometimes they decide who sits where, who marries whom, who drinks from which well.
The tenth Guru lived in a world full of such boxes. In one stanza of Akal Ustat he lists them, one by one, and then picks up the very word the boxes were built on and gives it to everyone.

teach.b: Here is the stanza, in paraphrase. Someone has become a shaven-headed renouncer; someone a yogi; someone a celibate student; someone an ascetic. Some are Hindus, some Muslims; some are Shia, some Sunni.
Then the line Sikhs quote today: recognize the whole human race as one. In Gurmukhi, manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo. Look at the word jat.

In everyday speech it's the word for caste, the box you're born into, the one that decided so much. The Guru keeps the word and widens it until it holds everyone. There is one jat, and it is the human one.
Notice the verb: pahichanbo, recognize. He doesn't say make everyone one, or pretend the labels aren't there. He has just named the renouncer, the yogi, the Hindu, the Muslim.
The labels are real. The call is to recognize what's under them.
Then the stanza turns toward God, in paraphrase: the Creator and the Merciful are the same; the Provider and the Compassionate are the same; there is no difference, and to think there is, is error.
He uses names for God from more than one language, side by side, and says they point to one.
In the Sikh tradition this line sits beside langar, where anyone eats sitting in the same row, and beside the gurdwara's open doors. It doesn't ask anyone to stop being who they are.
It asks them to see one family when they look around the room.

how: Sikhs quote 'manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo' from Akal Ustat when speaking about equality, and it is lived out in langar, where everyone eats together seated in the same rows.

o: one nation gathered under one ruler and flag
a single caste chosen to lead all the rest
recognizing all people as one human family

games.q: the stanza, piece by piece: tap the pairs.
p: the line lived with a plate

s: the stanza says labels like Hindu and Muslim aren't real
it names them, then asks us to recognize the one human race beneath them.
the Guru uses the word for caste to name all humanity
manas ki jat: the human jat, one for everyone.
the stanza says the different names for God point to different gods
Creator and Merciful, Provider and Compassionate: the same, it says.

games.q: you're the Guru, and you've just listed renouncers, yogis, Hindus, Muslims, Shia and Sunni. what's the next line?
o: tell them to drop their labels.
say one group has it right.
recognize the whole human race as one.
games.why: manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo: recognize, not erase, and rank no one.

practice: Bring to mind the people you'll pass today: a driver, a cashier, a coworker you find hard, someone whose head covering differs from yours, or who wears none.
Notice the box your mind puts each one in, without scolding yourself, and on the out-breath say inwardly: family. If you pray, rest in Waheguru between faces.

wordCard.voice: One human race. Manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo: recognize the whole human race as one, the tenth Guru's line in Akal Ustat. Today's word.

orig.s: ਮਾਨਸ ਕੀ ਜਾਤਿ ਸਬੈ ਏਕੈ ਪਹਿਚਾਨਬੋ
orig.say: MAA-nus kee JAAT sa-BAI AY-kai peh-CHAAN-bo
orig.note: recognize the whole human race as one: jat, the word for caste, made wide enough for all.

carryVoice: Your line: recognize one human family under every label. There is one jat, and it is the human one. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Dasam Granth, Akal Ustat 85 (koi bhaio mundia sanniasi ... manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo ... karta karim soi)
